It removes input entirely and works with any food, but camera recognition of food in a hot, steamy cavity and its accuracy and cost are open questions.
Solid-state RF is real and plausible, but the link to zero-learning-curve operation is weak since users don't notice magnetron warm-up.
Inverter-style power supplies already exist, and the user-facing simplicity gain is mostly indirect.
A coaxial feed is plausible and removes the mica cover, but it only slightly reduces maintenance and does little for operation.
A fully visible cavity is intuitive and novel, but ITO polymer would struggle with heat, power handling and shielding.
A molded shielded one-piece shell makes cleaning obvious, but polymer would cope poorly with heat, arcing and RF leakage.
Auto-sensing removes user input, but ultrasound doesn't propagate well into air-filled cavities or through food packaging, and it isn't a cheaper substitute for anything.
Plausible and simple, but it only handles power level and still leaves time and other decisions to the user.
Replacing the magnetron with IR lasers is radical, but surface-only heating, cost and safety make it implausible, and 'point and heat' needs aiming and still implies timing.
A ferromagnetic platen inside a microwave cavity conflicts with the RF field (arcing) and mainly adds browning, which does little for ease of use.
Peltier modules can't replace magnetron cooling or defrost effectively at this power level, and the link to simpler operation is weak.
Removing the power knob reduces decisions, but it is a feature removal rather than a radical idea, and full power alone overcooks many foods.
Weight-based auto-cooking really removes the need to set anything, though weight alone can't identify the food and the load cell adds cost.
A magnetic gasket would ease opening, but it does little for the learning curve and leaks or fails to meet safety interlock needs; a magnet seal is not a microwave choke.
Twisting a lid is a familiar action, but it is slower than a door, awkward for hot dishes, and tricky to seal against microwave leakage.
A holographic projection of food adds complexity and cost and does nothing to simplify operation, and the technology is impractical.
Thermoelectric waste-heat turntable is clever but barely affects user operation, and the power from a TEG would be marginal and the turntable would only turn once hot.

RF dielectric heating is real (used in industrial thawing and drying) and could give more uniform heating, but it is not simpler or cheaper for home use and does not directly reduce the learning curve.
A graphene-coated cavity cannot replace metal walls, which must reflect microwaves, and it does not by itself remove hotspots, though the goal of no food arranging is relevant.
A shape-memory alloy latch could give automatic gentle door release, which is simple to use, but it is a minor improvement and thermal actuation is slow.
An electrochromic window showing cooking state is feasible and intuitive, requiring no reading of a display, though it only addresses status feedback.
Self-cleaning air handling is plausible but barely touches operating simplicity, which is about controls rather than maintenance.
Wireless power removes plugging in, but a microwave's high power draw makes resonant inductive transfer impractical and it doesn't simplify the cooking interface.
A battery pack cannot realistically supply 1000W for long, and it does nothing to simplify the cooking controls.
A foldable solar panel can't power a microwave's wattage, and the claim of no buttons is unsupported and adds setup complexity.
Door-open-to-cook is an intriguing one-action concept, but piezoelectric hinge energy is orders of magnitude too small to cook anything.
A single color-zoned slider is intuitive, but zero-crossing SSRs can't easily drive a magnetron's high-voltage supply, and the substitution is only modestly radical.
A dissolving tablet timer is wildly novel and tangible, but dissolution times vary with temperature and it adds consumables and imprecision.
A touch-pad door release is easy to build and mildly simpler, but it adds little over a button and has safety and reliability concerns.
A ferrofluid RF seal is inventive, but it does little for ease of operation and has contamination and heat problems.
A door-wound spring turntable is a clever mechanical substitute for the motor, but it barely affects the user's learning curve and the spring's runtime is unreliable.
An external adapter does nothing for ease of operation, and a magnetron needs kilovolts, so a 48V input doesn't remove the high-voltage section.
A single large button replaces the keypad and dial, so there is nothing to learn, and it is easy to build, though not very radical.
A camera feed replaces the window, but it adds a screen to interpret and does not simplify operation, even though it is buildable.
A shape-memory vent flap is automatic and swaps out a part, but users never see it so it barely affects ease of use.
A conductive gasket in place of the choke is a plausible substitution, but it has no effect on how the user operates the oven and wear and leakage are concerns.
Optical sensing with a solid-state relay is plausible, but safety standards require redundant mechanical interlocks, and users see no change in operation.
Reed switches are feasible and used in some appliances, but the user-facing benefit for simple operation is minimal.
A resettable PTC avoids service calls, but magnetron thermal protection typically needs a reliable hard cutoff, and users rarely deal with resets anyway.
An SMA self-resetting overheat actuator is creative and plausible, though costlier than a bimetal and only indirectly tied to ease of use.
A polyfuse removes the need for fuse replacement, which is a real if small usability gain, and it is a well-established technology.
Auto-open door is simple and feasible but already exists on some models, and it addresses only the end of the cooking process rather than the controls.
Magnets can't safely replace the door interlock, which is a safety requirement, and the idea has little effect on the learning curve.
A disposable liner makes cleaning easier but has nothing to do with operation, and it raises concerns about fire risk and cost.
A molded plastic cavity is not compatible with microwave reflection and arcing requirements, and it relates to cleaning rather than operation.

Reading cooking instructions from the food package removes the need to use controls entirely, which fits the no-learning-curve goal well and is feasible with NFC, though it depends on packaging adoption.
Directly removes all inputs, which fits zero learning curve, but RFID can't sense food type or portion without tagged packaging, so feasibility is weak.
A shape-memory seal that opens when heated is a novel idea, but it risks microwave leakage and safety problems, and it barely affects operational simplicity.
A tumbling cavity is an unusual substitute for the turntable, but it would make a mess with liquids and does little for ease of use.
A microwave draws about 1kW, so solar charging is impractical, and it does not simplify operation.
Specific component swap, but it concerns weight and internals and has no effect on user operation; piezo transformers also struggle at magnetron power levels.
A mechanical pull-string timer is intuitive and simple, but it replaces only the timer and still leaves power choices; the pull-per-minute scheme is a bit awkward.

Removes timer setting in principle, but a thermochromic sticker in a microwave cavity responds poorly to food doneness, and users must still decide when to stop the oven, which makes the idea unreliable.
Place the food and walk away is the ideal zero-learning-curve operation, though optical sensing of doneness inside a steamy microwave is hard and the idea is not very cheap or simple.
Feasible and removes one control, but the user still sets time and the load cell adds cost instead of simplifying.
Opening the door is not the learning-curve problem, and a floor pedal is impractical for a countertop appliance, though it is hands-free.
Switchable opacity is plausible but does little to remove the learning curve, and it is a weak substitute for the mesh window.
An edible tray is a wild substitution, but it addresses cleaning rather than ease of operation.
A thermochromic sticker replaces timer setting with a visual cue, which is intuitive and cheap, though it needs consumable stickers and users must still stop the oven themselves.
A camera that picks the program directly removes the need to operate anything, but similar products already exist and the recognition is hard to get right.
A transparent OLED door gives clear feedback, but it is costly and the OLED would struggle with microwave and heat conditions.
Highly relevant and practical, but preset food buttons already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.
Sensor-based auto-stop removes the need to set a timer and is a real step toward zero learning, but it exists in some models and is only partly a substitution.
Feasible and cheap, but it only changes the done alert and does little to simplify operation.
A scent signal is novel and intuitive, but it is impractical, can't be reset, and has little effect on operation.
A glow coating would be dim and the idea has almost no bearing on ease of operation, though it is concrete.
Peltier venting is novel but has little bearing on operating simplicity and is inefficient for a microwave's heat load.
Ferrite beads are standard and have almost no effect on the user's learning curve.
Humidity-sensing auto-shutoff removes timer setting and is already proven in sensor-cook microwaves, though not radical.
Adaptive multi-feed heating removes the need for power settings, but it is complex and costly, and it is not a cheaper substitute.
A mode stirrer with no turntable is simple and easy to clean, but it only modestly helps operation and stirrers are already known.
Directly removes the learning curve with one-press cooking, though weight-sensing auto-cook is already seen in some products.
Imaginative, but a glowing coating does little for ease of operation and is questionable inside a microwave cavity.
A pull handle is intuitive and plausible, but it is a common design and only a small step toward simpler operation.
A mechanical done flag is simple and clear, but it addresses only the end-of-cycle signal and not operation.
A transparent graphene door is a neat substitution, but it is only loosely tied to ease of use and RF shielding is doubtful.
A single giant multi-press button directly removes the learning curve, though press-count mapping is somewhat arbitrary and not very radical.
A transparent display with a camera is eye-catching, but it adds complexity and does little for operation simplicity; it is also hard to build with a metal mesh door and heat.
A radical iris opening with hand-wave activation is intuitive, but sealing microwave leakage with an iris is extremely hard, and the idea is costly rather than a simple substitution.
A familiar lid motion is feasible, but it only changes the door and does not simplify the controls, which is where the learning curve is.
A GaN solid-state RF source gives continuous power and is real technology, but the user benefit for simplicity is indirect and the cost is high.
A door bezel that rotates to set time is a single obvious action and fairly novel, though it adds door mechanism and wiring complexity and may be less precise than a knob.
Easier cleaning is nice, but it barely affects operation learning, and silicone may not suit microwaves or cook evenly without rotation.
Very radical, but an IR camera and e-paper on the door adds cost and complexity and does little for simple operation.
A mechanical flag is cheap and familiar from toasters, but it only signals completion, which is a small part of operation.
A pictogram slider for power is intuitive and simple to build, but it only covers power and not time.
Removes fuse replacement but is mostly hidden from users and barely affects operational simplicity.
A cost and part-count tweak that has no bearing on ease of operation.
A paper shell is a cosmetic change unrelated to operation and is questionable near heat, grease and steam.
A tambour door is intuitive and eliminates the latch, but sealing microwave radiation with flexible slats is very difficult.
A single timer-style knob with automatic power directly delivers a no-learning-curve interface and is easy to build.
A pull-handle drawer is intuitive and plausible, but it only addresses opening and does little for operating the timer or power.
Voice for power levels needs no learning in principle, but it covers only power, adds cost, and can misrecognize in a noisy kitchen.
+/- buttons with an LED bar are simple and very feasible, but common and not radical, and the LED replacement is more complex than a knob.
A rotary dial timer is a quirky retro idea that is familiar to some elderly users but unfamiliar to younger ones, and it is slower to operate.
A floor pressure plate that opens the door is wild and workable, but it risks accidental opening and doesn't simplify cooking operation.
Novel scent-based end signal, but it only addresses the notification and not operation, and scent emitters add cost, consumables and unreliable perception.
A vibration motor in the handle is easy to build, but it only replaces the bell and does little to simplify operation.
A projected icon interface on the counter is intuitive and replaces physical controls, though it needs a touch-sensing projector, and glare and heat in a kitchen are problems.
Gesture control removes buttons, but gestures must be learned and are not obvious, and it is costlier than the buttons it replaces.
Looking at an icon to start is radical and requires no learning, but eye-tracking is costly, accidental starts are a safety risk, and it doesn't cover time or power settings.
A picture-based dial directly removes the need to learn numbers and times, though icon dials are not very radical and fixed times may not suit every portion.
Auto power selection eliminates settings in principle, but reliably identifying food from RF reflection is technically difficult and the mechanism is only loosely described.
Passive cooling is a concrete substitution, but it does little for ease of operation and is hard to fit into a cheap microwave.
A resettable PTC cutout is plausible and spares users a manual reset, but the benefit to operation is marginal.
Reed switches are a realistic, well-specified swap, but they barely affect how simple the oven is to operate.
